To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intrathoracic LES displacement decreases LES pressure and LES competence.

vagotomy at the canine LES results in a decrease in LES pressure, which is further decreased by intrathoracic placement of the LES; that fundoplication combined with abdominal replacement restores LES pressure and function, and that LES pressure and function are associated with the length of the LES.
intrathoracic placement of the LES results in a decrease in both resting pressure and response to compression, whereas restoration of the LES below the thorax improves both parameters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the position of the LES on its function, and with the restoration of gastroesophageal function after vagotomy.
the influence of the position of the lower esophagus on its function.
the effect of change of position of the lower esophagus on the function of its sphincter.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LES is a dynamic muscular sphincter, the function of which can be influenced by the position of the LES in the chest or abdomen.

LES competence is maintained in the thorax by an active process, and that restoration of competence by operations that replace it below the diaphragms is dependent on both the pressure-generating capacity of the LES and on its position in the abdominal cavity.
the LES has a high degree of intrinsic competence, but that this is dependent on the position of the sphincter in the thorax or abdomen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

intrathoracic LES displacement results in decreased LES pressures and competence, and that fundic-wrap and abdominal LES replacement improve LES function by restoring the LES to its normal intrathoracic location.
intrathoracic LES displacement is detrimental to sphincter competence, and that the fundic-wrap operation is most effective in restoring LES function in the dog.
the function of the LES depends on both intrathoracic location and the length of the high pressure sphincter zone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LES is a pressure zone, not just a valve, and it is important to restore the pressure zone in addition to replacing the valve.
the LES can be restored to competence by replacing it below the diaphragms.
the LES is not a sphincter in the usual sense of that term.
